analysis.one_liner: Replaces the consumer bankruptcy system with a single chapter that lets households erase more debt, including student loans.
analysis.headline: The Senate introduced the bill on December 9, 2020 and sent it to the Judiciary Committee, which never held a hearing or vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have torn up the current consumer bankruptcy system and replaced it with one new chapter, Chapter 10, for people with up to $7.5 million in debt. It would have repealed Chapter 13 (the repayment-plan track) and ended individual use of Chapter 7 liquidation. Instead, every household would get a single, simpler process: debtors whose income is below about 135% of their state's median would owe little or nothing and get their debts erased quickly, while higher-income debtors would pay a share of their excess income over up to three years. It would let people reduce home mortgage and car loan balances to what the property is actually worth, wipe out student loan debt on the same terms as credit card and medical debt, and get a discharge once every six years. It also created a Consumer Bankruptcy Ombuds at the consumer protection bureau to police how debtors are treated.
analysis.who_benefits: Households overwhelmed by debt — often from job loss, medical bills, or student loans — who today face a complicated, expensive two-track system. Low- and middle-income debtors could get a faster, cheaper discharge, keep a car worth what it actually sells for, catch up on a home mortgage without paying penalty interest and fees, and erase student loan debt that is currently almost impossible to discharge. People of color, who the bill's findings say are pushed disproportionately into the worst part of the current system, would get a single uniform process.

how_it_helps.text: Creates a single Chapter 10 bankruptcy for individuals with up to $7.5 million in debt, replacing both Chapter 7 liquidation and Chapter 13 repayment plans, with minimum payments calculated from the debtor's income and assets — debtors with no payment obligation get an immediate discharge.

Lets debtors modify home mortgages (avoiding foreclosures the bill's findings say happen today without reducing financing costs), reduce car loan balances to the car's market value, and cure mortgage defaults without paying interest on arrearages or penalty fees.

Makes student loan debt dischargeable on equal terms with most other debt, and lowers the cost of filing by simplifying paperwork, which the bill's findings say keeps many people who need bankruptcy from affording counsel.

Adds consumer protections including a Consumer Bankruptcy Ombuds at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, stronger remedies against collectors who violate the discharge, and new rules for credit reporting and debt collection.

Closes loopholes the bill's findings say let wealthy, well-counseled debtors shield assets, and sets a sliding scale so debtors well above median income repay a share of their excess income over three years.

analysis.who_pays: Consumer lenders recover less when debts are erased. Credit card issuers, private student loan lenders, medical debt buyers, and collection agencies would see more debts discharged and fewer multi-year repayment plans. Mortgage lenders and servicers would lose penalty interest on arrears and could no longer block or stall a borrower's catch-up plan. Auto finance companies would be paid based on the car's market value instead of the full loan balance. Lenders can be expected to argue that these losses would be passed back to all borrowers through higher interest rates and tighter credit.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit card, student loan, mortgage, and auto lenders

drawbacks.text: Lenders' losses could be passed to borrowers as higher interest rates or tighter credit, which is the standard objection creditors raise to eroding their bankruptcy recoveries.

Debtors with income above roughly 135% of their state median would face a mandatory payment schedule of 15% to 150% of their excess income — some higher earners would repay more over three years than they would under today's Chapter 7, and no one can get a second discharge for six years.

Repealing two long-established chapters and rebuilding the system in one stroke would require a massive transition for bankruptcy courts, trustees, and attorneys, and the bill's own funding provisions (new fees, revised trustee compensation) would have to work as designed to keep the courts running.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the households the bill targets — people with little income and heavy debt — the gains are large and concrete: a cheaper, faster discharge, manageable car loans, a real chance to save a home, and student loans that can actually be erased. The costs fall mostly on creditors and, indirectly, possibly on future borrowers through pricing. The trade-off for middle- and upper-income filers is more mixed: a single uniform system is fairer, but some would pay more than under current law. The design is coherent and heavily detailed, not a rushed proposal.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the closing weeks of the 116th Congress, sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, and the committee never took it up — no hearing, no vote — so it simply expired when the session ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Elizabeth Warren introduced the Consumer Bankruptcy Reform Act of 2020 on December 9, 2020, with Senators Durbin and Whitehouse as the only cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on the Judiciary the same day.
No further action was taken: the Judiciary Committee never held a hearing or a vote, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumer lenders — credit card issuers, student loan and mortgage companies, auto finance firms, and debt collectors — keep the current bankruptcy rules, under which more debt survives and student loans are nearly impossible to erase.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumer lenders, who keep current bankruptcy rules

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and became its lead sponsor on December 9, 2020.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on December 9, 2020 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All three senators behind the bill were Democrats, no Republican joined it, and the bill never advanced far enough for any vote or recorded opposition.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers and unsecured consumer lenders
industries.note: More debts would be discharged sooner and student loan balances would become erasable, cutting what these lenders collect from households in distress. Their interest in blocking the bill ran directly against the debtors it would help.
The bill ends the special protection that has made private student loans nearly impossible to discharge, a protection the bill's findings say never lowered borrowers' financing costs.
Debtors could modify home mortgages and cure defaults without paying interest on arrears or penalty fees, and lenders could not block a confirmed residence plan while payments stay current.
Car loans could be written down to the vehicle's actual market value, eliminating the premium lenders collect today when owners are underwater on a car they need to get to work.
Stronger discharge enforcement, new collection rules, and faster discharges would shrink the pool of old debts that can be profitably chased.

A single-chapter system with new fee and trustee-compensation structures would reshape their business — some work (Chapter 13 plans) disappears, while simplified filings and court funding through fees change the rest. Their clients are the debtors the bill helps.
